E0798.summary: In the later Table Talk, Atwood links the Horizontal with fixation and with 'latitude'.
E0798.body: Atwood, in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), speaks of “the fixation by the Horizontal; altitude and latitude” [APP ¶173]. The record suggests Horizontal Magnetism is what effects fixation, set beside 'latitude'. The text gives no fuller definition.

E0799.summary: In Apuleius' tale as Atwood cites it, the form Lucius regains with the goddess's help when he sheds the ass's hide.
E0799.body: The voice is the quoted Apuleius. The goddess promises Lucius that “by whose assistance you will return to the Human Form” [II.4 ¶17]. Return to the Human Form means shedding the ass's hide.

E0800.summary: The human will, which Atwood says has corroborative efficacy when it acts in concert with its Final Cause to fulfil it.
E0800.body: Atwood speaks of “the corroborative efficacy of the Human Will, acting in concert with its Final Cause to fulfill it” [III.4 ¶28]. The record gives the Will a supporting power in the work only when it acts in concert with its Final Cause.

E0801.summary: Author of Poetry of Science, cited by Atwood as showing that modern science admits the nature of light is unexplained.
E0801.body: Atwood cites Hunt's *Poetry of Science* in support of her point that modern science admits it has not explained the nature of light [I.2 ¶47, I.2 n45]. She uses him as a supporting authority.

E0802.summary: Lully's name for the subject, a clear compounded water like argent vive; also, in a cited cosmogony, the 'enormous first-born' of Chaos's primeval parent.
E0802.body:
Two quoted voices use the term.

Lully names the subject Hyle and describes it: “it is a clear compounded water, most like in substance to argent vive” [I.2 ¶29]. In the readers' summary of the passage it also flows on earth, is generated in every compound from the substance of the air, and is extremely heavy [I.2 ¶29].

In the account Atwood attributes to the metropolitan of Memphis, the primeval parent of Chaos “brought forth her enormous first-born Hyle” [III.3 ¶46].

The records do not say whether the two uses are meant to be the same thing.

E0803.summary: A hymn to Mercury, its source not named, that Atwood quotes as illustrating Mercury 'with like allusion'.
E0803.body: Atwood quotes a hymn, without naming its source, as illustrating Mercury “with like allusion”: “Hear me, O Mercury, and Son of Maia; the bright expositor of things!” [I.2 ¶36].

E0804.summary: The teacher who, Atwood says, taught Synesius the occult truths of the philosophy.
E0804.body: Atwood names Hypatia as the person who taught Synesius the occult truths of the philosophy [I.1 ¶27]. That is all the record says about her.

E0805.summary: Atwood's word, applied to Democritus' occult researches and to Plato's whole philosophy with its mystic, recondite character.
E0805.body: Atwood applies the word to Democritus' occult researches, such as making precious stones (“these and such-like hyperphysical researches” [I.1 ¶12]), and to Plato: “But the whole philosophy of Plato is hyperphysical” [I.1 ¶17]. There it goes with the mystic, recondite character of Plato's philosophy. The text gives no definition.

E0806.summary: Atwood's recurring, undefined term, apparently for the substantial ground of a being, which must be dissolved and renewed and is to be redeemed as reason's true objective reality.
E0806.body:
The voice throughout is Atwood's. She never defines the word, so its meaning has to be gathered from how she uses it.

**The natural self that must die.** She speaks of “The self-willed hypostasis of nature must die” so that nature's universal being can evolve [I.3 n53]. Elsewhere the condition of new life and of growth into consciousness is “a dissolution of the whole natural born hypostasis” [III.1 ¶50].

**The soul's ground in darkness.** While “her hypostasis continues in darkness” the soul is in Hades. It is “the alone eternal hypostasis to be redeemed from thence”, that is, from the oblivious realms of generation [II.3 ¶36].

**Reason's true object.** Reason's true Hypostasis is her objective reality: “it is her true Hypostasis, for which, as Isis for Osiris, she is constantly seeking, her objective reality in the Great Unknown” [II.3 ¶46]. The 'new world' made with furnace and glass is glossed as “a new hypostasis, and a new stone” [II.3 ¶52]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), once the Chimaeras are destroyed, what remains is “the simple Hypostasis or radix of the reason that seeks” [APP ¶171], so the Hypostasis is equated with the radix (root) of the seeking reason.

**Transformation.** “the whole hypostasis was converted finally through faith into the identity of substant light within” [III.1 ¶11]. At the Soul's return “a new hypostasis is created out of the darkness to abide” [III.3 ¶10].

**Matter and Essence.** She uses the word of the First Matter (“such an hypostasis is in the beginning without all affirmation” [III.2 ¶57]) and of the Eternal Essence perceived intellectually: “an hypostasis unwearied, untamed, and never failing” [III.2 ¶59].

**Adjective forms.** In the Vital Spirit, active and passive power are joined in a 'hypostatic union', and there are “the hypostatic principles of attraction and repulsion and circulation” [III.3 ¶9]. The Initiates' regard of God “was not extraneous but hypostatical, as of like to like” [II.4 ¶40].

The common thread, as these uses suggest, is a substantial ground or root of being: in its natural, self-willed state it must be dissolved, and in its true state it is sought and renewed.

E0807.summary: The working of the essences in life, which Atwood says is proved by those who enter experimentally within.
E0807.body: Atwood refers to “the hypostatic action and passion of the working essences in life” [IV.4 ¶4]. Those who enter experimentally within prove it. It is not further explained.

E0808.summary: The reality the consciousness in Hades is taught to aspire to but cannot find by itself through the darkness.
E0808.body: Atwood speaks of “that Hypostatic Reality towards which it is instructed evermore to aspire” [II.3 ¶29]. 'It' is the consciousness in Hades, which cannot find this reality by itself through the darkness.

E0809.summary: Body, soul and spirit, taken as three relations of one life, distinguished only as agent, patient and offspring.
E0809.body: Atwood identifies “body, soul, and spirit --- the three hypostatic relations” [III.3 ¶67]. They are relations of one life, born one from another and distinguished only as agent, patient and offspring. On transmuting these relations, see hypostatic union.

E0810.summary: In the cited Vaughan, the union of celestial nature, aerial spirit and the soul's aura, which are one in substance.
E0810.body: The voice is the quoted Vaughan. He names three things, the celestial nature, the aerial spirit and the soul's aura: “These three, being but One substantially, admit of a perfect hypostatic union” [III.3 ¶27]. The Quadrature is achieved “by a transmutation of the hypostatic relations” [III.3 ¶30], which the readers render as an exchange of active and passive. Atwood also speaks in her own voice of a 'hypostatic union' of active and passive power in the Vital Spirit [III.3 ¶9].

E0811.summary: That which is triply introverted and multiplied by the circulatory medium throughout life to manifest the magistery.
E0811.body: Atwood speaks of the “multiplication of the hypostatic unit by the circulatory medium throughout life” [IV.2 ¶37]. The unit is triply introverted, and its multiplication manifests the magistery. It is not further defined.

E0812.summary: The union in which Light overcomes darkness, which Atwood offers as the proper antidote to inbred evil.
E0812.body: Atwood speaks of “overcoming darkness by Light in the hypostatical alliance” [IV.4 ¶17]. She presents this as the proper antidote to inbred evil, and does not explain it further.

E0813.summary: A Neoplatonist whose Life of Pythagoras and On the Mysteries Atwood cites often and with approval, on Theurgy, prayer, divine union, purification and the Tetractys.
E0813.body:
Atwood spells the name Iamblicus, Iamblichus and Jamblicus. She lists him among the Alexandrian revival figures who professed Theurgic and Hermetic knowledge [I.1 ¶27]. She also lists him among the Neoplatonists whose surviving writings show the nature of the Mysteries, the disease of the Spirit and its clarification [II.2 ¶9]. He is consistently a supporting authority, and she does not dispute him.

**Life of Pythagoras.** Wisdom “is truly a science which is conversant with the first and most beautiful objects”, objects that do not decay and by participation in which other things are beautiful [II.1 ¶39, II.1 n37]. The uninitiated mind is like “dense thickets, which are full of briars”, and souls must be cleansed before they receive doctrine, as in the dyer analogy [II.2 ¶11, II.2 n12]. Nearby, Theurgic rites follow immutable intellectual canons, and the mundane spirit fashions the soul's powers [II.2 ¶13, II.2 ¶15]. Chap. 28 is the source of the verse on the Tetractys: “Whence all our Wisdom springs, and which contains Perennial nature’s fountain, cause, and root” [III.3 ¶34, III.3 n23].

**On the Mysteries.** Theurgists became partakers in Wisdom “by certain ineffable and sublime media that Theurgists became cognizant partakers in the Wisdom of true Being”, not by contemplation or representation [II.2 ¶3, II.2 n7]. Union comes from divine media and Synthemata, not from intellectual perception, through “the perfect efficacy of ineffable works”. Atwood endorses this [II.4 ¶31, II.4 n23]. The gods give true illuminations, not phantasms: “By no means therefore, says Iamblichus, does Divinity either transform himself into phantasms” [II.4 ¶29, II.4 n20]. He also describes the effect of the divine vision on initiates with the image of fishes [II.4 ¶19, II.4 n12]. Pure Matter, “being connascent with the gods by whom it is imparted, will doubtless be an entire and fit receptacle for the manifestation of Divinity” [III.2 ¶49, III.2 n39]. Theurgists consulted the divine intellect only on the purification, liberation and salvation of life [III.1 ¶12, III.1 n9]. Atwood uses him to judge Hermes' lost books by the surviving Asclepian Dialogues and Poimander [I.1 ¶7, I.1 n9].

**Prayer.** In defending prayer, she writes: “Prayer, according to Iamblicus, was divided into three classes”. She takes from him that prayer is necessary in sacred operations and purifies the soul [III.4 ¶24, III.4 n26].

E0814.summary: Icarus and his father, used as an illustration within Basil Valentine's allegory.
E0814.body: Icarus and his father Daedelus appear as an illustration within Basil Valentine's allegory [III.2 ¶19]. The record says nothing more.

forms: Idea of the Good, the Pure, and the True
E0815.summary: The alluring object all inwardly worship, the progeny of Divine Intellect, shining dimly through sense and selfishness as a guide.
E0815.body: Atwood writes: “The Idea of the Good, the Pure, and the True is the alluring object which we all innerly worship” [IV.3 ¶52]. She calls it “the progeny of Divine Intellect, immortal and strong --- even Moral beauty”, which equates it with Moral beauty. It “ever shines attractively --- our Polar Star” through the mists of sense and selfishness, though obscurely, and so serves as a guide [IV.3 ¶52].

E0816.summary: The ideal measure of excellence, which Atwood says modern literal conceits have stripped bare.
E0816.body: Atwood complains of “conceits which have stripped the Ideal Standard of all excellency” [IV.4 ¶29]. The context links these conceits to modern literal readings.

E0817.summary: The universal forms of Nature from which essence takes form, and the conceived pattern that the alchemical agent images as the will directs.
E0817.body:
In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood equates “Ideas or the universal forms of Nature” [APP ¶37] and calls them that from which essence receives form.

In the main text, the Idea is the pattern a work images. In the ordinary arts the product remains “to image, not the motive instigatory, but the Idea” [III.4 ¶8]. In Alchemy the agent images what is conceived as the will directs: “to image the conceived Idea” [III.4 ¶9].

E0818.summary: A co-operation without which, Atwood says, we can never learn how Nature works; she contrasts it with reasoning from sense.
E0818.body: Atwood writes: “nor shall we ever learn, without Identic co-operation, how Nature works” [IV.4 ¶12]. She contrasts it with reasoning based on the senses and does not define it further.

E0819.summary: The indestructible substance that survives the dissolution of the whole being: true grain, root of the world, and seed of this world and the next.
E0819.body: Atwood describes it as the indestructible substance that survives when the whole being is dissolved. It renews the dissolved parts, and once freed it is Protean and changes colour [III.2 ¶20]. It is “the seed not only of this world but o the next” [III.2 ¶20]. She equates it with the true grain (“adepts have concluded this Identic Salt to be the true grain”) and with the root of the world (“this mystical substance, this root of the world”) [III.2 ¶20].

E0820.summary: The source in which the soul, in awe, begins to perceive herself, and into whose consciousness she passes through regeneration.
E0820.body: Atwood writes that the soul “begins to perceive itself in that Identic Source” [II.3 ¶37]. In the same paragraph she speaks of “the reminiscent consciousness of her Causal Source” [II.3 ¶37]. This apparently names the same source, into whose consciousness the soul passes through regeneration.

E0821.summary: The spirit that rises pure, bright and contrite from its primaeval element when the conflicts end, subject only to its own Law.
E0821.body: Atwood writes: “the Identical Spirit arises, pure, bright, and contrite, from its primaeval eleemtn” [III.1 ¶68]. It does so at the end of the conflicts, and afterwards it is subject only to its own Law. The text does not explain the word 'Identical'.

E0822.summary: Atwood's term for knowing without separation of subject and object, a state reason enters through regeneration; also used of individual selfhood, which must pass into universal accord.
E0822.body:
The voice throughout is Atwood's.

**A state of knowledge.** Once the inner light is fixed and the outer spirit made pliant, reason may “become into that Identity by which the powers of the Universal Nature are made manifest and intrinsically understood” [I.3 n8]. Here subject and object are not separated: the soul knows “but absolutely, in Identity” and becomes consubstantial with what she knows [II.4 ¶42].

**Made in regeneration.** Identity is “made in the regeneration by the reprocedure into experience out of the dissolute void of life when artificially induced” [III.2 ¶16].

**Selfhood.** Atwood also uses the word for individual selfhood. She speaks of “the exterminating fiat of our Identity”, which hides the exemplary Logos [III.3 ¶79]. In the final step, by the energy of faith, “the Identity passes into universal accord” and leaves separable selfhood behind [IV.3 ¶60].

**Ambiguity.** The Wisdom is reached by “the searching and proving of His own Identity” [IV.4 ¶27]. The text leaves unclear whose Identity 'His' refers to.

The two senses, the goal of knowing and the separate self to be transcended, sit side by side in the text.

E0823.summary: In the later Table Talk, Atwood's special sense of idolatry: forming the First Matter to a particular end of one's own, or stopping at any finite gift instead of the Universal.
E0823.body: Both records come from the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer) and are in Atwood's voice. In one, idolatry is man specificating and qualitating from his own mind, forming the First Matter for a particular end: “in this consists the true idolatry against which the Bible so strongly protests” [APP ¶37]. In the other, the work offers gifts and finite ends, and “you may stop in any of them; if you do, you commit idolatry.” [APP ¶135]. Stopping there instead of seeking the Universal means the will is creating idols for itself.

E0824.summary: The philosophers' fire, which the later Table Talk distinguishes from Vulcan (Motion), the stirrer up of the fire.
E0824.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), Atwood says: “Vulcan is not the fire, the ignis Philosophorum, but the stirrer up of the fire.” [APP ¶129]. Vulcan is identified there as Motion. Nothing more is said about the fire itself. (Latin *ignis Philosophorum*: 'fire of the Philosophers', our translation.)

E0825.summary: The poem as Atwood quotes it, for mutual aid, for the passing on of healing virtues, and (in Table Talk) for the connate spirit deprived of its understanding spirit.
E0825.body:
Atwood uses the Iliad for illustration only.

Book 10 illustrates the mutual aid of two: “By mutual confidence and mutual aid” [III.1 ¶45, III.1 ¶46, III.1 n52].

Book 11 illustrates how healing virtues are handed on: “Such as sage Chiron, sire of pharmacy, First taught Achilles, and Achilles thee” [IV.3 ¶33, IV.3 n11].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer), the episode after the death of Patroclus illustrates the connate spirit deprived of its understanding spirit [APP ¶109].

E0826.summary: In Iamblicus as Atwood cites him, what the first of the three classes of prayer pertains to.
E0826.body: The voice is the quoted Iamblicus, as Atwood reports him: “The first, recapitulates our author, pertains to Illumination” [III.4 ¶24]. 'The first' is the first of the three classes of prayer.

E0827.summary: The self as likeness of its divine source, which one reflects into for self-knowledge and passes beyond toward the Archetype.
E0827.body: Atwood speaks of “that great and miraculous mystery of our Image” [III.3 ¶25]. On the readers' account, the self is a likeness of its divine source and is to be reflected into for self-knowledge. One “passes from himself as an image to the Archetype” [III.3 ¶26].
